children.html: Associations between femininity ideology and body appreciation among British female undergraduates
• aDepartment of Psychology, University of Westminster, London, UK
• bDepartment of Psychology, HELP University College, Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia
Article history: Received 2 October 2009 Received in revised form 17 November 2009 Accepted 21 December 2009 Available online 18 January 2010
Keywords: Body appreciation Gender ideology Femininity Ideology Scale Gender roles

The current study examined the relationships between gender ideology and body image in a sample of British female undergraduates. A total of 135 women completed the Body Appreciation Scale (BAS), the Femininity Ideology Scale (FIS), and provided their demographic details. Inter-item correlations showed significant negative correlations between body appreciation scores and the total FIS score, FIS subscales of Purity and Stereotypic Images and Activities, and respondent BMI (rs -.17 to -.26). A multiple linear regression showed that Stereotypic Images and Activities and participant BMI alone explained 10.0% of the variance in body appreciation. These results are discussed in relation to previous studies showing mixed associations between gender role orientation and body image and eating disorders.

Body image is a multidimensional concept that includes an individual's cognitions, feelings, and perceptions related to their own body (Thompson, Heinberg, Altabe, & Tantleff-Dunn, 1999). Spurred by evidence of associations between body image disorders and impaired self-esteem, reduced social effectiveness, and disordered eating (e.g., Grogan, 1999; Polivy & Herman, 2002), some researchers have sought to understand individual differences in antecedents of negative body image (e.g., Swami, Hadji-Michael, & Furnham, 2008a). One relatively neglected factor in this research is gender ideology, which refers to an individual's internalisation of societal and cultural beliefs about gender roles (Levant, 1996; Pleck, 1995; Thompson & Pleck, 1995).

It seems plausible that the internalisation of such beliefs should be associated with body image among women, given the influence that gender role orientation has on interpersonal development (Pleck, 1981, 1995). Indeed, previous studies have shown that gender role orientation is related to body dissatisfaction (Jackson, Sullivan, & Rostker, 1988; Lewis & Johnson, 1985; Swami et al., 2008a) and disordered eating (for a review, see Murnen & Smolak, 1997). An important limitation of these studies, however, is that they have tended to measure gender role orientation as an individual's position along a diffuse continuum of masculine–feminine

dimensions (after Bem, 1977). In contrast, recent work has sought to move beyond viewing gender roles in terms of such gendertyped personality traits, and stresses the multidimensional nature of gender ideology (e.g., Levant, Richmond, Cook, House, & Aupont, 2007; Payne, 2006).

An important advance in this direction was the development of the Femininity Ideology Scale (FIS; Lehman, 2000), which assesses the degree to which respondents endorse traditional femininity ideology (that is, beliefs about how women should act), rather than the extent to which a woman self-reports that her behaviours, feelings, and cognitions conform to expectations about femininity (Levant et al., 2007). The FIS consists of five factors that represent different dimensions of traditional femininity ideals, namely Stereotypic Image and Activities (women should maintain a particular physical appearance and image that is consistent with societal ideals), Dependency/Deference (women should play dependent and deferent roles in relation to their male relations), Purity (women should demonstrate chastity and passive roles), Caretaking (women should seek to attain feminine ideals of motherhood), and Emotionality (women should have an emotional affinity for domestic-related work).

In the present study, we sought to examine the associations between the FIS factors and body appreciation (that is, a positive orientation towards one's body). We selected the latter variable, as opposed to traditional measures of negative body image for two reasons. First, although body image has been acknowledged as a multi-dimensional construct (e.g., Thompson et al., 1999), very few studies have measured an individual's positive acceptance of, respect for, and protection of their body (Avalos, Tylka, &

Wood-Barcalow, 2005). Second, and when viewed in this way, positive body image may be expected to have different correlates than negative body image; certainly, no previous work has examined the associations between body appreciation and the FIS factors, which the present study sought to overcome.

Given that the Stereotypic Image and Activities factor measures concepts that are most closely related to body image, we expected a negative correlation between this factor and body appreciation. That is, we expected that women who held more traditional beliefs about physical appearance and image would have lower body appreciation scores. Another FIS factor that was expected to show a significant association with body appreciation was Purity. Specifically, we expected that women who held more traditional beliefs about a chaste ideal and passive sexual roles were expected to have lower body appreciation. In contrast, we did not expect to find significant correlations between body appreciation and the FIS factors of Dependency/Deference, Caretaking, and Emotionality.

The participants of this study were 135 women enrolled in various undergraduate degree courses at a university in Greater London. Participants ranged in age from 17 to 51 years (M = 23.74, SD = 5.78) and in self-reported body mass index (BMI) from 17.15 to 33.27 kg/m2 (M = 22.15, SD = 2.80). Of the total sample, 45.2% were of European Caucasian descent, 23.7% were of Asian descent, 11.9% were of African Caribbean descent, and 19.3% were of some other ancestry. The majority of participants were single (51.1%), while others were in a relationship (37.0%), married (10.4%), or of some other marital status (1.4%).
2.2.1. Body Appreciation Scale (BAS; Avalos et al., 2005)

The BAS is a 13-item scale that measures favourable opinions of one's own body, acceptance of the body in spite of imperfections, respect for the body, and the rejection of unrealistic ideals. All items were rated on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = Never, 5= Always). Responses on all 13 items were averaged to obtain an overall body appreciation score, with higher scores reflecting greater body appreciation. Previous work has shown that the BAS has a unidimensional structure when completed by Western women (Avalos et al., 2005; Swami, Stieger, Haubner, & Voracek, 2008b) and has good test–retest reliability and construct and discriminant validity (Avalos et al., 2005). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha for this scale was .89.

The FIS is a 45-item scale that measures the degree to which respondents endorse traditional femininity ideology along five dimensions (see above). All items were rated on a 5-point Likerttype scale (1 = Strongly disagree, 5= Strongly agree) and factor scores were computed by taking the mean of items associated with each subscale of the FIS (higher scores reflect more traditional gender ideology). It is also possible to compute a Total Traditional score by computing the mean of all 45 items. Previous work has shown that the FIS has high internal consistency and good construct and discriminant validity (e.g., Lehman, 2000; Levant et al., 2007). In the present study, Cronbach's alpha for the five subscales were: Stereotypic Image and Activities, .88; Dependence/Deference, .85; Purity, .88; Caretaking, .89, and; Emotionality, .83. For the Total Traditional score, Cronbach's alpha was .93.

Participants were asked to provide their demographic details consisting of age, ethnicity, religion, marital status, height, and weight. The latter two items were used to calculate participants' BMI (kg/m2 ).

Once ethical approval for the study was obtained from the relevant university ethics committee, participants were recruited on an opportunistic basis. In practice, this meant approaching potential participants at various campus sites (e.g., libraries, cafeterias, communal spaces) and inviting them to take part in a study on body image. Once participants provided informed consent, they were provided with a five-page questionnaire, which they completed anonymously and individually. All participants took part on a voluntary basis and were not remunerated for their participation. Once they returned their questionnaire to the experimenter, they were verbally debriefed.

Descriptive statistics (Ms. and SDs) and inter-item correlations for all target variables are reported in Table 1. As can be seen, body appreciation was significantly and negatively correlated with Stereotypic Images and Activities, Purity, the Total Traditional score, and participant BMI, although it should be noted that these correlations were weak (rs -.17 to -.26). We next performed a multiple linear regression with body appreciation as the dependent variable and the five FIS factor scores, age, and BMI as predictor variables. Results showed that the regression was significant, F(7, 134) = 3.09, p = .005, Adj. R2 = .10, with Stereotypic Images and Activities
(st. b = -.25, t = 2.24, p = .027) and BMI (st. b = -.18, t = -2.19, p = .031) emerging as the only significant predictors.

The results of this study showed that more traditional femininity ideology was associated with lower body appreciation. This can be seen in the significant negative correlation between body appreciation and Total Traditional scores, as well as the negative correlation between body appreciation and two subscales of the FIS (Purity and Stereotypic Images and Activities). At first glance, these results were perhaps not surprising, particularly in relation to the significant association between body appreciation and Stereotypic Images and Activities scores, given that the latter measures components most closely related to body image. However, we suggest that our results represent an advance on the available literature because of our measurement of femininity ideology: where previous work has tended to measure gender role orientation, our study is (to our knowledge) the first to operationalise femininity ideology in terms of respondents' endorsements about how women should act.

Indeed, it is noteworthy that previous work that have used measures of gender role orientation (rather than internalisation of gender ideology) have not reported consistent associations (e.g., Cantrell & Ellis, 1991; Hepp, Spindler, & Milos, 2005; Johnson, Brems, & Fischer, 1996; Meyer, Blissett, & Oldfield, 2001). Furthermore, a thorough understanding of the nature of relationships between gender role orientation and body image remains difficult because of inter-study differences in samples and the operationalisation of gender role orientation (Hepp et al., 2005). As such, our results offer a contribution to this literature, showing significant associations between gender ideology and body appreciation.

Of course, it is important to note that the associations seen in the present study were weak, and femininity ideology and participant demographics only explained 10.0% of the variance in body appreciation. A stronger correlation may have been expected between body appreciation and the Stereotypic Images and Activities factor, but it is important to remember that the items included in the latter measures both endorsement of beauty ideals (e.g., 'A woman should have a petite body') as well as beliefs about culturallyprescribed activities for women (e.g., 'It is more appropriate for a female to be a teacher than a principal'). Thus, the multidimensional nature of this factor may help explain the weak correlations uncovered in the current study.

In terms of limitations, it should be noted that our sample consisted of undergraduates and, as such, it may not be possible to generalise these findings to wider populations of women. Nevertheless, student samples are perhaps most problematic when the issues being investigated have little relevance to those involved. In the present study, issues relating to gender ideology and body image are appropriate, particularly as this group evidences high rates of negative body image. In addition, although we have interpreted our findings in the most plausible manner, it is difficult to infer causational relationships using correlational designs. Finally, while our interest was in examining the relationships between

femininity ideology and body appreciation specifically, this possibly obscured other relevant psychological traits that may mediate reported associations, such as social status, sexism and hostility toward women, and sexual orientation.

Overall, it appears that gender ideology may play a significant role in shaping women's attitudes toward their bodies. Further research should pay greater attention to femininity ideology in the aetiology of body image disorders, as addressing issues related to gender ideology may help promote greater body satisfaction. That is, promoting more egalitarian and non-traditional gender ideology may be expected to result in more positive body image among women (see also Swami et al., submitted for publication).
